◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The Word became flesh' is, for Cyril, the dogmatic foundation of the Miaphysite confession received by Tewahedo: one incarnate nature of the Word, indivisibly united from two natures (divine and human) without confusion. Against the Nestorian reading that finds two persons or two natures-after-union, Cyril insists the union is hypostatic and indivisible. The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Cyril on the 3rd of Hamlē for this defense.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria De Incarnatione Verbi §8 (c. 350 AD)

'And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth' — Athanasius marks ho Logos sarx egeneto (the Word became flesh) as the SINGLE most important verse for the entire incarnational-treatise. The egeneto (became) is genuine becoming — not Docetic-appearing, not Arian-creature-clothing, not Nestorian-association-with. The Word remained-what-he-was (eternal-divine-Logos) and BECAME-what-he-was-not (genuine-human-sarx). The eskēnōsen (dwelt — literally 'tabernacled') connects to the OT shekinah-dwelling and to Jn 2:21 ('he spake of the temple of his body'). The doxan-as-of-monogenous (glory-of-only-begotten) is the visible-Shekinah-glory of the incarnate-Word that Peter, James, John see at the Transfiguration (Mt 17:1-8, 2 Pet 1:16-18). This is Athanasius's signature-verse: DI §54's famous 'He was made man that we might be made God' is the soteriological-corollary of Jn 1:14's incarnational-fact. The Tewahedo Lǝdat-creed cites Jn 1:14 first among the Johannine prologue verses.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'No man hath seen God at any time; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He hath declared Him' is for Cyril the dogmatic statement of the Son's unique revelatory office. 'In the bosom of the Father' (eis ton kolpon tou Patros) Cyril reads not spatially but as expressing intimate co-substantiality and eternal mutual indwelling. The Son's revelation is not derivative testimony but the Father's self-disclosure in His own Word. Against Eunomian rationalism (which claimed direct knowledge of the divine essence), Cyril here grounds Christian epistemology in the Son's mediation: we know the Father only through the Son who eternally knows Him.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On John the Baptist's self-identification as 'the voice of one crying in the wilderness' (citing Isa 40:3), Cyril develops the patristic distinction between Voice (phone) and Word (logos): the Baptist is the audible preparation for the eternal Word's manifestation. The Voice is heard, then ceases; the Word abides forever. The 'wilderness' Cyril reads typologically: not merely the Judean desert but the spiritual barrenness of pre-Incarnational humanity awaiting the Word's coming. The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors the Baptist as the 'lamp of Christ' on the 30th of Hidar, preserving this Voice-Word distinction in its liturgical hymnody.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' Cyril reads as the typological climax of the entire Hebrew sacrificial economy: the Paschal lamb of Exodus, the lambs of the daily burnt offering, the Isaianic lamb led to the slaughter — all converge in the Baptist's pointing finger. The 'taketh away' (airon) Cyril stresses as present-tense ongoing action: the Lamb's atoning work is not a single historical moment but the perpetual offering perpetually applied through the Church's eucharistic representation. This sacrificial-eucharistic reading is foundational to the Tewahedo Anaphora's offertory prayers.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending and remaining (menon) on Him' Cyril reads with characteristic pneumatological depth: the Spirit's *remaining* (not just descending) distinguishes Christ from all the prophets, on whom the Spirit had come and departed. The Spirit's permanent indwelling of the incarnate Word is the source of every subsequent gift of the Spirit to humanity — what Christ possesses by nature, He communicates to the baptized by participation. Cyril here grounds his entire pneumatology in the Jordan event: the Holy Spirit's mission to the Church flows from His abiding upon the Son.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Cyril carefully defends Christ's address to His mother at Cana ('Woman, what have I to do with thee?') against any reading that would imply disrespect. 'Woman' (gynai) is for Cyril a formal address of honor, not familiarity-refused; the question is rhetorical, situating the miracle within His Father's appointed timing rather than maternal pressure. Mary's authority remains intact (she immediately directs the servants to obey Christ) — the verse establishes the principle that Christ's miracles proceed from the Father's will, not human request, even when that human is His own mother. Tewahedo Marian veneration preserves this delicate balance.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Fill the waterpots with water' Cyril reads as the typological pivot of the entire Cana sign: Christ deliberately requires human cooperation (the servants' labor of filling) before the divine transformation. The six stone waterpots — used for Jewish purification rites — Cyril reads as the six days of creation (the imperfect order awaiting completion), or as the Old Covenant's purification economy awaiting Christ's New Covenant fulfillment. The water-to-wine transformation prefigures the eucharistic transformation: the elements remain (water/bread), but their inner reality is changed by Christ's word.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On 'This beginning of miracles did Jesus' Cyril notes the programmatic placement: a wedding-feast miracle inaugurates the public ministry, signaling that Christ's mission is nuptial in character — He has come to wed humanity to divinity in His own flesh. 'Manifested forth His glory' (ephanerōsen tēn doxan autou) Cyril reads as the proleptic revelation of the cross's glory: the Cana glory and the Calvary glory are one glory, the glory of the eternal Word visible in His incarnate works. The disciples' belief that follows is the first-fruits of the entire Church's faith.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' is for Cyril a Christological saying of central importance: the temple in question is not Herod's structure but Christ's body, and the active agent of the Resurrection is the Son Himself ('I will raise it up' — egerō auton). Against subordinationist readings that would make the Resurrection a passive event done TO Christ by the Father, Cyril insists on the Son's active agency: the Word raises His own assumed humanity through the divine power that is His own by nature. This is the dogmatic root of the Tewahedo Easter Anaphora's doxology of the Risen Christ as agent of His own resurrection.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

John's interpretive aside — 'He spake of the temple of His body' — provides Cyril his exegetical warrant for body-as-temple typology that runs throughout his John commentary. The Old Covenant temple (with its court of Gentiles, holy place, holy of holies) prefigures the structure of the incarnate Christ: His flesh is the new court where Gentiles enter, His soul the new holy place, His divinity the new holy of holies indwelt by the Father. This temple-Christology extends to ecclesiology: the Church as Christ's body inherits the temple typology, with baptism replacing circumcision as the gateway and the eucharist replacing the daily sacrifice as the perpetual offering.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Except a man be born again (anōthen), he cannot see the kingdom of God' is for Cyril the doctrinal axis of the entire Nicodemus pericope. The Greek 'anōthen' carries the double sense of 'again' (temporal) and 'from above' (spatial); Cyril preserves both: the new birth is at once a second temporal beginning AND a heavenly-origined event, not produced from human sources. This rebirth is necessary not as supplement to natural birth but as substitute for it on the order of grace: what natural birth gives (mortality, sin-inheritance, alienation from God) the rebirth replaces (incorruption, adoption, communion). The verse is the locus classicus for the Tewahedo doctrine of baptism as ontological renovation.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit' Cyril reads as the dominical institution of baptism: the two elements (water and Spirit) are inseparable, not sequential. Against the Messalians and other spiritualizing groups who would dispense with water and rely on a purely interior Spirit-experience, Cyril insists that the Spirit binds Himself to the water-sign in the Church's sacramental administration. The water is not merely symbolic accompaniment but the divinely-chosen visible vehicle of the Spirit's invisible regenerating act. This sacramental realism is the textual ground of the entire Tewahedo baptismal theology.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit' Cyril reads as Johannine confirmation of the doctrine of original sin: flesh begets only flesh, and the natural process of generation cannot transmit anything beyond the conditions of fallen creaturehood. Only the Spirit's begetting communicates spiritual life. Cyril is careful here to distinguish his reading from Manichaean dualism: 'flesh' is not evil per se but is wounded and unable to ascend to spiritual life without supernatural elevation. The Spirit's birth does not destroy the flesh but heals and elevates it — preparing for the bodily resurrection.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On 'The wind bloweth where it listeth' Cyril makes the most of the Greek pneuma's double sense (wind / spirit): the meteorological observation grounds the pneumatological doctrine. The Spirit's working in regeneration is sovereign (chooses its own subjects), audible-in-effects (the voice is heard), but invisible-in-cause (we cannot trace its origin or destination). Against Pelagian readings that would make human will the operative cause of regeneration, Cyril insists the Spirit's freedom is primary: regeneration is sovereign gift, even where it is mediated through baptism's prescribed channels. The Spirit who fills the prescribed channels is not bound by them.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'No man hath ascended up to heaven, but He that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven' is a verse Cyril uses to defend the *communicatio idiomatum* — the communication of attributes between Christ's divine and human natures in His one Person. The Son of man is 'in heaven' even while speaking to Nicodemus on earth: the divine attribute (omnipresence) is predicated of the human Person (Son of man) by virtue of the hypostatic union. Against Nestorian dilution (which would assign heavenly attributes only to the Logos-Person and earthly attributes only to the human-Person), Cyril here grounds the Miaphysite confession in Christ's own Johannine self-witness.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's typological self-reference — 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up' — Cyril develops with characteristic typological care. The bronze serpent was a likeness of the agent of death (the serpent) elevated as the means of healing; Christ on the cross is the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom 8:3) elevated as the means of salvation. The 'must' (dei) Cyril reads as expressing not external necessity (the schemes of His enemies) but the Father's eternal redemptive will to which the Son freely conforms. The Tewahedo Holy Week liturgy preserves this typological reading prominently.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On the most-cited verse in the Gospel — 'For God so loved the world, that He gave His only-begotten Son' — Cyril builds the Athanasian-Cappadocian Trinitarian framework: the Father's love for the world is so radical that He gives not merely a creature or a prophet but His own consubstantial Son. The 'gave' (edōken) refers both to the Incarnation (the eternal Son's mission into flesh) and to the cross (the giving up to death) — the two are one redemptive movement. 'Only-begotten' (monogenēs) excludes any creaturely sonship: the Son's relation to the Father is unique, eternal, and inseparable. Cyril notes that 'the world' (kosmos) here means the whole of humanity, not the elect-narrowly — universal scope of love, particular efficacy of salvation through faith.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's promise to the Samaritan woman — 'Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life' — Cyril reads pneumatologically: the water is the Holy Spirit Himself, given through Christ as His own gift to those who receive Him. The water's spring inside the believer (pēgē hydatos hallomenou) figures the Spirit's permanent indwelling, distinguished from the Old Covenant prophetic intermittent inspiration. 'Springing up' (hallomenou) carries the sense of leaping, dynamic ascent — the Spirit's indwelling is not static container but living source of theosis.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth' Cyril reads as the abrogation of the geographic-cultic restriction (Jerusalem temple / Mt. Gerizim) in favor of pneumatic-Christological worship. 'In spirit' is for Cyril 'in the Holy Spirit' (the worshipper's pneumatic transformation), and 'in truth' is 'in the Truth that is Christ' (Jn 14:6). True worship after the Incarnation is therefore Trinitarian: to the Father, in the Spirit, through the Truth-Son. This passage grounds the Tewahedo liturgical doctrine that the Anaphora's prayer is itself the Spirit's praying through the Church to the Father, mediated by the Christological elements.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'God is a Spirit' (pneuma ho theos) — Cyril reads this as ontological statement (the divine nature is spiritual, not material) and as missiological imperative (those who would worship a spiritual God must be spiritually transformed). Against the Anthropomorphites who attributed bodily form to God, Cyril insists the verse settles the question: God has no parts, no extension, no spatial location. Yet against any Hellenizing collapse of God into pure abstraction, Cyril preserves the personal-relational character: the Spirit-God is the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit — three Persons in one spiritual essence. Worship 'in spirit and in truth' is therefore the only worship corresponding to God's actual mode of being.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My meat is to do the will of Him that sent me, and to finish His work' Cyril reads as Christ's self-disclosure of the perfect harmony between His human will and the Father's eternal will. Against the Apollinarian denial of Christ's human soul (or against any reading that would make Christ's will merely divine), Cyril here recognizes that Christ has a genuinely human will, but it is so perfectly conformed to the Father's will that 'doing the Father's will' becomes His characteristic sustenance — what physical food is to bodily life, the doing of the divine will is to Christ's incarnate human life. This is the seed of the dyothelite-anticipation that becomes explicit in later Greek theology, though Cyril himself does not yet use those terms.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The Samaritans' climactic confession — 'This is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world' (ho sōtēr tou kosmou) — Cyril emphasizes as the proleptic Gentile recognition of Christ's universal salvific scope. The Samaritans, themselves marginal to Jewish covenant identity, become the prototype for the Gentile inclusion that will mark the post-Pentecost Church. 'Saviour of the world' is for Cyril a title both universal (Christ saves the world, not merely a portion) and particular (each person is saved as individual within that universal scope). The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Photine (the traditional name of the Samaritan woman) on the 26th of Hidar — her witness to her village becomes the first apostolic missionary act recorded in John.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's command to the paralytic — 'Rise, take up thy bed, and walk' — Cyril reads as the threefold pattern of every healing the Word performs in the soul: resurrection from spiritual death (rise), taking up the burden of one's former weakness as instrument rather than master (take up thy bed), and active progress in the new life (walk). The thirty-eight years of paralysis Cyril typologically links with the thirty-eight years of Israel's wilderness wandering (Deut 2:14) — both the individual and the people are healed by direct sovereign address, not by mediating ceremony or stirred-pool waiting. The Sabbath setting prepares Cyril's larger argument: Christ exercises the Father's authority over the Sabbath because He is consubstantial with the Father.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' (heōs arti) — Cyril reads as one of the most decisive anti-Arian sayings in the Gospel. The Sabbath rest of Gen 2:2 did not mean God ceased operating (providence is unbroken); Christ here claims the same uninterrupted operative power that belongs to the Father. The 'and I' (kagō) refuses any subordination: the Son's working is co-equal, co-eternal, co-extensive with the Father's. The Jews' immediate reaction (5:18: they sought to kill Him for 'making Himself equal with God') confirms they understood the claim correctly. Cyril uses this verse against the Eusebian semi-Arians of his own day who would dilute the Son's operative parity with the Father.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The Jews' interpretation — that Christ was 'making Himself equal with God' (ison heauton poiōn tō Theō) — Cyril takes as inspired witness, not hostile misreading. Even Christ's opponents recognized that calling God 'my Father' (idion Patera) in this manner was a claim to consubstantial equality, not adoptive sonship. Cyril notes the Greek 'idion' (own/proper) carries the sense of natural-not-merely-adoptive: the Son's relation to the Father differs in kind, not just degree, from any creature's. This verse is one of Cyril's strongest scriptural anchors against Arian and Eunomian readings — even the unbelieving witnesses confirm the orthodox reading.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do' Cyril reads with extreme care against Arian misreading. The 'can do nothing of Himself' is NOT a statement of weakness or subordination but of perfect Trinitarian harmony: the Son's operations are inseparable from the Father's because of their consubstantial unity. The 'seeing' is not perceptual observation (as if the Son had to watch what the Father did) but eternal mutual indwelling of co-equal Persons. 'What things soever He doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise' (homoiōs) Cyril stresses: not subordinately, not differently, but identically — every divine work belongs to all three Persons indivisibly.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'As the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom He will' — Cyril takes the absolute power of the eschatological resurrection as the supreme proof of consubstantiality. To raise the dead is a work exclusively divine; for the Son to share this power without limit means He shares the divine nature. 'Whom He will' (hous thelei) Cyril emphasizes: not a delegated authority to be exercised within constraints, but sovereign personal choice — the same will that the Father exercises. The verse also establishes the personalist character of resurrection: Christ raises individuals by His sovereign decision, not as automatic effect of cosmic process.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son' Cyril reads as the eschatological consummation of the Father-Son economy: the Father's universal judgment is exercised through the incarnate Son, who because of His shared human nature is uniquely fit to judge humanity. The 'committed' (dedōken) Cyril carefully distinguishes from any subordinationist reading: this is not a delegation of authority the Father lacks the will to exercise directly, but the manifestation of the eternal Trinitarian order — every operation 'from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit' (Cyril's standard formula). This verse grounds Cyril's later argument (in the Twelve Anathemas) that the man-God Christ, not a separate human judge, presides at the Last Day.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.16 (c. 350 AD)

'That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him' — Athanasius marks hina pantes timōsi ton Huion kathōs timōsi ton Patera (that all should honor the Son EVEN AS they honor the Father) as the HOMOTĪMION (equal-honor) prooftext. Equal-honor is owed-by-creatures only to one equal-in-nature (homoousios) with the Father; therefore the kathōs (EVEN AS, in-the-same-manner-as) directly entails homoousion. Any reduction of the Son to creature-status would make this equal-honor idolatrous; the Word's-own-claim therefore-positively-requires divine-essence. Pairs with Phil 2:10 (every-knee-shall-bow at-the-name-of-Jesus) as the canonical equal-divine-worship pair.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He that heareth my word, and believeth on Him that sent me, HATH everlasting life' Cyril reads as one of the strongest realized-eschatology pins in the Gospel: eternal life is not merely promised for the future but present possession of the believer through faith. 'Is passed from death unto life' (metabebēken — perfect tense, completed action with continuing result) confirms the present reality: the believer has ALREADY transitioned from the death-realm to the life-realm. This is not denial of future bodily resurrection (which Cyril affirms strongly) but recognition that the spiritual-ontological transition has already occurred for those united to Christ by faith. The verse grounds Cyril's sacramental realism: baptism enacts what faith receives.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'As the Father hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son to have life in Himself' is for Cyril a critical text for the Son's natural-not-derived divinity. The 'given' (edōken) is not temporal grant (as if the Son did not always possess what He now has) but eternal communication of essence — the Father eternally communicates to the Son the same divine life He has from Himself. To 'have life in Himself' (echein zōēn en heautō) is the divine attribute par excellence: not life received from elsewhere, but life as one's own essence. The Father has it without source; the Son has it from the Father, yet equally and eternally. This is Cyril's most precise statement of the Cappadocian-Athanasian doctrine of eternal generation.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me' Cyril takes as the dominical hermeneutical principle: the Hebrew Scriptures are properly read only when read Christologically. Against Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament and against the Jewish rejection of its messianic-Christological reading, Cyril positions the verse as Christ's own self-witness: He IS the proper subject of the Scriptures. 'Ye think' (dokeite) is gentle correction: searching the Scriptures for eternal life apart from recognizing Christ in them is futile — the life they testify to is the life He brings. This verse grounds the entire Alexandrian typological hermeneutic.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me' Cyril reads as Christ's authoritative claim to be the proper object of every Mosaic prophecy. The verse establishes the principle that Moses and Christ stand in continuity, not discontinuity: rejection of Christ is rejection of Moses (and conversely, true reception of Moses leads to Christ). Cyril uses this verse against any Manichaean or Marcionite reading that would oppose the Testaments; he also uses it against any Jewish reading that would treat Mosaic obedience as sufficient apart from Christological reception. The Tewahedo Pentateuch readings in the Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase preserve this Cyrilline unity by always pairing Torah readings with their Christological NT fulfillment.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On the multiplication of loaves Cyril notes the deliberate eucharistic prefiguration: Christ TOOK the loaves, gave THANKS (eucharistēsas), and distributed. The four-fold pattern (take / bless / break / give) that becomes the Mass Cyril sees inaugurated here — the feeding of the five thousand is the sign that points to the institution at the Last Supper and the perpetual continuation in the Anaphora. The crowd's hunger Cyril takes typologically: humanity hungers for the bread of eternal life which only Christ can give; physical hunger is the symptom of the deeper spiritual hunger. The Tewahedo Anaphora's preparation prayers preserve this typological reading explicitly.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life' Cyril reads as Christ's hermeneutic for understanding the previous miracle: the loaves were sign, not substance — the substance is the eucharistic bread that gives eternal life. 'Which the Son of man shall give unto you' (dōsei — future tense) Cyril emphasizes: pointing forward to the institution of the eucharist, not to repeat-feedings of physical bread. 'For him hath God the Father sealed' Cyril reads as the Spirit's anointing that makes Christ's human nature the perpetual source of the bread of life — the seal of the Spirit on the incarnate Son is what makes the eucharistic gift possible.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the bread of life' (egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs) — the first of Christ's great 'I AM' sayings in John — Cyril reads as both ontological self-disclosure and sacramental promise. The 'I am' echoes the divine name (Ex 3:14: ego eimi ho ōn); the 'bread of life' identifies the specific mode of Christ's gift to His Church. 'He that cometh to me shall never hunger, and he that believeth on me shall never thirst' Cyril takes as the perfect parallel between coming-to-Christ (sacramentally: through baptism into His body) and believing-on-Him (fiducially: through saving faith) — neither alone, but both together produce the perpetual satisfaction of spiritual hunger and thirst.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of Him that sent me' Cyril reads against any reading that would set the Son's will in opposition to the Father's. The 'not mine own' (ouch hina poiō) does not deny that the Son HAS a will (Apollinarian denial), nor does it imply imperfect alignment requiring submission. Rather, Cyril notes the Son's INCARNATE human will is now in question: as man, the Son receives the Father's will and acts upon it; as God, His will is identical with the Father's by nature. This is one of Cyril's earliest articulations of what later dyothelite theology would systematize: two wills (divine + human) in one Person, perfectly aligned.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him' Cyril reads as the Johannine doctrine of prevenient grace. The Father's 'drawing' (helkysē) is the operative work of grace that precedes and enables human response to Christ; without it, no one comes. Cyril is careful here against Pelagian readings: the verse strictly excludes natural human capacity to come to Christ apart from divine initiative. Yet the 'drawing' is not coercive — Cyril (following the classic patristic distinction) reads it as the Father's drawing through the Spirit's inward attraction, which the human will may still resist (against later Augustinian readings that would make it irresistible). This passage grounds the Eastern Christian doctrine of synergism: grace initiates, the will cooperates.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world' is for Cyril the central eucharistic-Christological text in the entire Gospel. The bread Christ gives IS His own flesh — the personal Word's true flesh, not a metaphor or symbol, but the incarnate body offered on the cross and now communicated through the eucharist. 'For the life of the world' confirms the universal scope of the offering — not for the elect alone, not for the Jews alone, but for the kosmos. Cyril uses this verse as the textual foundation for his doctrine of eucharistic realism that becomes determinative for all subsequent Greek and Oriental Orthodox theology.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink His blood, ye have no life in you' Cyril takes with full sacramental seriousness: this is not metaphor but ontological condition. The eucharistic eating-and-drinking is the necessary means by which the life of the incarnate Word is communicated to the believer's body and soul. Against any spiritualizing reading that would dissolve the verse into mere faith-receptive metaphor, Cyril insists the verse means what it says: the actual flesh and blood of Christ, sacramentally present, must be actually received. 'Ye have no life in you' (ouk echete zōēn en heautois) is the privative consequence of refusing the eucharistic gift. This is the locus classicus of Cyril's eucharistic theology that the Tewahedo Anaphora preserves verbatim.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day' Cyril reads as the eucharistic guarantee of bodily resurrection. The flesh of Christ communicated to the believer's body becomes the seed of the resurrection body — Cyril's standard formula is that the eucharist is the 'medicine of immortality' (pharmakon athanasias, from Ignatius). The 'I will raise him up' is Christ's personal promise tied to the eucharistic reception: the body that has received the Body of Christ has within it the seed of eschatological transformation. This verse anchors Cyril's distinctive contribution to eucharistic theology: the sacrament does not merely commemorate or symbolize, it actually communicates the resurrection life.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'For my flesh is meat indeed (alēthōs), and my blood is drink indeed' Cyril takes as decisive against any reading that would weaken eucharistic realism. The Greek 'alēthōs' means 'truly / really / actually' — Christ here explicitly disqualifies any metaphorical or symbolic interpretation of His preceding words. Against the gnostics of his own era and against any anticipatory spiritualizing readings, Cyril insists: TRULY flesh, REALLY blood — the eucharistic gift IS what it appears to be on the level of substance, even while remaining bread and wine to the senses. This is Cyril's clearest articulation of what later Western scholasticism would call the doctrine of real presence (without scholastic categories of substance/accidents).

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'It is the Spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing' Cyril famously handles with great care against capernaitic misreadings that would take 'eating the flesh' as cannibalistic physical consumption. The 'flesh' that profiteth nothing is fleshly-mode-of-understanding, not the actual flesh of Christ (which gives life). The verse means: receiving the eucharist with merely carnal comprehension — as if Christ's body were divided physically among communicants like ordinary food — is profitless. Only Spirit-quickened reception receives the gift as it truly is. This is Cyril's careful pneumatological qualification of his strong eucharistic realism: the realism is true, but its appropriation is spiritual, not crudely physical.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My doctrine is not mine, but His that sent me' Cyril carefully defends against Arian misreading. The 'not mine' does NOT deny the Son's possession of the doctrine but identifies its source: the Son's teaching is not innovative or independent but is the eternal teaching of the Father, possessed by the Son by nature (consubstantial communication of all divine attributes including wisdom-teaching). Cyril notes the parallel to 5:30: 'I can of mine own self do nothing' — both texts speak of perfect Trinitarian harmony, not of any inferiority in the Son. The Son's teaching IS the Father's teaching because the Son IS the eternal Word who speaks the Father's mind.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'If any man will do His will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God' Cyril takes as the dominical statement of moral epistemology: knowledge of divine truth is conditioned on willingness to obey. Against any purely intellectual approach to theological knowledge (which would make speculation independent of holiness), Cyril here grounds the patristic axiom: theology requires askesis. The 'will to do His will' (thelē to thelēma autou poiein) Cyril emphasizes as primary disposition; the cognitive recognition follows on it. This verse becomes the textual root of the entire Eastern Orthodox tradition that knowledge of God presupposes purification of the nous through ascetic practice.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Judge not according to the appearance (kat' opsin), but judge righteous judgment' Cyril reads as Christ's hermeneutical principle for theological discernment. The Jews were judging based on surface considerations (the Sabbath violation appeared); Christ calls them to deeper judgment (the inner meaning of the law as service to humanity). For Cyril this verse is the dominical warrant for the typological-spiritual exegesis of the Old Testament: the appearance of the text (the literal-historical sense) must be supplemented by the righteous judgment (the spiritual-Christological sense) that recognizes Christ in every passage. This grounds the entire Alexandrian hermeneutical method.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink' Cyril notes the timing with care: on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, when the temple's water-libation ceremony reached its climax, Christ stood up to offer Himself as the true reality the ceremony only prefigured. The water libation pleaded for the autumn rains; Christ offers the Living Water of the Spirit that gives eternal life. The 'standing' (statheis) and 'crying' (ekraxen) Cyril takes as proleptic posture of the eschatological Christ — standing as the judge, crying as the herald of salvation. The Tewahedo Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase Anaphora prayers for the Holy Spirit echo this passage's invitation.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly (koilias) shall flow rivers of living water' Cyril reads as the pneumatological promise: the Spirit indwelling the believer becomes a perpetual source overflowing to others. The 'rivers' (plural — potamoi) signify both abundance (not merely a trickle) and diversity (different charisms flowing through different believers). The 'belly' (koilias) Cyril interprets as the heart in its biblical-Hebraic sense — the seat of personal life — not the digestive organ. The Tewahedo baptismal liturgy preserves this verse as one of the dominical promises connected to the chrismation that immediately follows baptism: the Spirit poured out becomes the believer's own source of life-giving witness to others.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

John's interpretive aside — 'This spake He of the Spirit, which they that believe on Him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified' — Cyril takes as decisive for the post-Pentecost-character of the Spirit's full gift. 'Was not yet' (oupō ēn) does NOT mean the Spirit did not exist (Cyril rejects this Origenist misreading) but that the Spirit had not yet been GIVEN in the new-covenant fullness — that giving awaits the Cross-Resurrection-Ascension sequence ('glorified' here meaning the entire paschal exaltation, not merely Resurrection appearance). After Pentecost the Spirit indwells the Church permanently as in 7:38; before Pentecost the Spirit comes intermittently as in the Old Testament prophets. This verse anchors Cyril's pneumatology of progressive economy.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The temple officers' report — 'Never man spake like this Man' (oudepote elalēsen houtōs anthrōpos) — Cyril takes as inspired witness from unwilling sources. The very men sent to arrest Christ become the heralds of His unique authority: they cannot perform their task because the sheer weight of His word disarms them. Cyril notes the linguistic precision: not merely 'never has anyone spoken' but specifically 'never man' (anthrōpos) — implying recognition that more than a mere man speaks here. The verse becomes for Cyril the historical-witness confirmation of the Logos's incarnate authority — even those resistant to faith bear unintended testimony to it.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.30 (c. 350 AD)

'Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am' — Athanasius marks prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi (before Abraham came-to-be, I AM) as Christ's DIRECT ARTICULATION OF THE DIVINE NAME (Exo 3:14 egō eimi ho ōn). The tense-juxtaposition is crucial: Abraham came-to-be (genesthai, aorist-of-becoming, creaturely-temporality) versus I AM (eimi, present-of-eternal-being, divine-timelessness). The Word's pre-Abrahamic-existence is not 'older-than-Abraham' (which would be creaturely-comparative) but in-a-different-tense entirely — eternal-being-versus-temporal-becoming. The Jewish-interlocutors recognize the blasphemy-claim and pick up stones to kill him (Jn 8:59), confirming they-understood the egō-eimi as divine-self-identification.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.1-25 (c. 350 AD)

'I and my Father are one' — Athanasius devotes much of Contra Arianos III (chs 1-25) to the proper-exegesis of egō kai ho patēr hen esmen, the singular-most-decisive Arian-controversy verse. Athanasius establishes (a) hen is NEUTER (hen esmen = 'we are one-thing'), not MASCULINE (eis esmen = 'we are one-person'); the verse therefore affirms one-essence (homoousion) with TWO-distinct-Persons (Father and Son both subjects of the plural-verb esmen). (b) The verse cannot be reduced to mere moral-union-of-wills because the listening Pharisees correctly understood it as a divinity-claim and prepared to stone Jesus for blasphemy (Jn 10:31, 33). (c) Christ's appeal to Ps 82:6 in his self-defense (Jn 10:34-36) is an a-fortiori argument: if covenant-mediating-judges can be called 'gods' analogically, the eternal-Son consubstantial-Word can be called 'God' properly. The Tewahedo Christological-confession at every Anaphora preserves Jn 10:30's neuter-hen ontological-unity-of-essence formula.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's response to Lazarus's sickness — 'This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby' — Cyril reads with characteristic providential precision. 'Not unto death' does NOT deny the impending physical death of Lazarus (which occurs and is graphically described) but rather denies death's TERMINUS character: death will not be the final word, glory will. 'That the Son of God might be glorified' Cyril takes as showing Christ's deliberate ordering of the entire sequence — including the delay (vv. 6-7) — toward the eschatological self-revelation. The Tewahedo Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase preserves this providential reading in its prayers over the dying: every sickness is potentially the occasion for divine glory.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's announcement — 'Our friend Lazarus sleepeth (kekoimētai)' — Cyril notes establishes the patristic-liturgical vocabulary for Christian death: the dead 'sleep' (koimēsis, Latin dormitio) rather than 'die' in the pagan-tragic sense. The verb implies awakening; sleep is not termination but pause. Cyril builds his entire doctrine of Christian death from this: the cemetery (koimētērion) is etymologically a 'sleeping-place' awaiting resurrection. The disciples' literal-minded misreading ('if he sleep, he shall do well') Christ corrects (v. 14: 'Lazarus is dead'), but Cyril preserves the original metaphor as theologically correct: Lazarus's death is a sleep precisely because of what Christ is about to do to it.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the resurrection, and the life' (egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē) — the fifth of Christ's 'I AM' sayings in John — Cyril reads as the climactic ontological self-disclosure of the Word in His resurrection-power. Christ does not say 'I cause' resurrection or 'I bring' resurrection but 'I AM' resurrection — He is Himself the active principle of bodily restoration from death. 'And the life' Cyril takes as the deeper ontological foundation: resurrection-of-the-dead presupposes life-as-such which Christ IS by nature. Against any reading that would make Christ a powerful intermediary, Cyril insists the verse predicates of Christ what is predicable only of God. This is the textual heart of Cyril's resurrection-Christology.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die' Cyril treats with careful eschatological precision: 'never die' (ou mē apothanē eis ton aiōna) does NOT deny the universal experience of bodily death (which Christians clearly continue to experience) but denies death's POWER as a permanent severance from God. The believer dies physically but is not dead spiritually; the body sleeps but the soul lives in Christ; the resurrection at the last day reunites and consummates. This realized-eschatology reading is paired with the future-eschatology of v. 24-25; Cyril holds both together as the proper Christian doctrine of death and resurrection — fully realized in part now, awaiting full consummation.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The shortest verse in the Gospel — 'Jesus wept' (edakrysen ho Iēsous) — Cyril expounds at length as decisive for orthodox Christology against three errors at once. (1) Against the Apollinarian denial of Christ's true human soul (Christ wept with real human grief, possessing human affections). (2) Against the Docetist denial of true incarnation (the tears were real tears, not theatrical). (3) Against any Stoic reading of impassibility-applied-to-Christ (Christ's incarnate nature genuinely felt sorrow). Yet Cyril carefully preserves the divine nature's impassibility: the WEEPING is predicated of the one Person via the assumed humanity, not of the divine essence in itself. This is Miaphysite Christology applied to a single verse — load-bearing for Tewahedo dogmatic theology.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God' Cyril reads as the principle that faith is the epistemic condition for perceiving divine glory. Martha's prior hesitation ('by this time he stinketh') is gently rebuked; Christ reframes the situation: belief is not response to the miracle but PRECONDITION for properly perceiving it. The 'glory of God' Cyril takes here as denoting both the resurrection-miracle about to occur AND the eternal Glory of the Son which the miracle makes visible. The Tewahedo liturgical posture before consecration — the faithful stand in reverent silence, the deacon calls 'Let us attend' — embodies this Cyrilline principle: faith first, vision second.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's prayer of thanksgiving — 'Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me' — Cyril carefully defends against any subordinationist reading. The prayer is not informational request (as if the Son needed to ask the Father for power) but liturgical-pedagogical: spoken for the benefit of the bystanders to manifest the unbroken Trinitarian communion. 'Thou hast heard me' (in the perfect tense — ēkousas) Cyril reads as evidencing the eternal mutual-knowing of Father and Son: the Father has eternally 'heard' because the Son and Father share one divine knowledge. The prayer is the incarnate Word's pedagogical disclosure of what is always already eternally true.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Lazarus, come forth' (Lazare, deuro exō) — Cyril notes the cosmic significance of the imperative addressed to a corpse. The verb 'come forth' presupposes a hearer capable of obeying; Christ speaks to Lazarus as already living, since His Word IS life-giving. The naming 'Lazarus' Cyril takes as theologically precise: Christ calls only this one out of the tomb (else, the patristic tradition observes, all the dead would have risen). This personal-specific calling prefigures the eschatological resurrection where each believer is called by name. The Tewahedo Easter Anaphora's prayer 'arise, my soul, from the dust' explicitly echoes this Lazarus pattern.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit' Cyril reads at multiple levels simultaneously. Most literally, it is Christ's self-prediction: His death is the necessary condition for the harvest of redemption. Typologically, it prefigures every Christian death-and-resurrection (baptism as participation in His pattern). Pneumatologically, the fruit-bearing is the Spirit's work in the Church proceeding from the cross. Cyril notes the grammatical force: not 'IF it die' (uncertain) but 'IF it die' (conditional contrast) — death is the NECESSARY price of the harvest, not an unfortunate possibility. This verse anchors Cyril's theology of redemptive suffering both for Christ and for those united to Him.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Now is my soul troubled (tetaraktai); and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour' Cyril expounds as a critical Christological text. The troubling is real (against Docetism — the human nature genuinely faced its passion with distress), yet does not master the divine will (the Son's choice to drink the cup is unimpaired). 'What shall I say?' Cyril reads as rhetorical question, not actual confusion — the Son's deliberation is pedagogical for the bystanders' instruction. The verse establishes that the assumed human nature carries authentic affective response WITHIN the perfect alignment of the incarnate will with the Father's eternal will. This is Cyril's most careful handling of the Gethsemane-style problematic in his John commentary.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world (ho archōn tou kosmou toutou) be cast out' Cyril reads as the cosmic dimension of the cross's victory. Satan's claim over fallen humanity (rooted in the legal title acquired through Adam's transgression) is broken by Christ's death, which the prince of this world wrongly exercised against a sinless victim — thus losing his lawful claim over all who unite to Christ. The 'now' (nun) Cyril emphasizes as the kairos-moment of the cross: not at some future eschatological judgment, but already in Christ's death-and-resurrection, the cosmic decision is rendered. This Christus-victor reading is central to the Tewahedo Easter liturgy's triumphal language.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'And I, if I be lifted up (hypsōthō) from the earth, will draw all men unto me' Cyril unpacks the deliberate double sense of 'lifted up': it refers at once to the cross (literal elevation on the wood) AND to glorification (exaltation to the Father's right hand) — the two are one redemptive movement in John's theology. 'Draw all men' (pantas helkysō) Cyril reads as universal scope of the saving intention: not only Jews, not only those present, but all humanity drawn by the magnetic power of the crucified-and-glorified Word. John's parenthetical note (v. 33: 'this He said, signifying what death He should die') is Cyril's textual confirmation that the cross is integral to the drawing.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness' Cyril reads as the final Johannine 'I am' statement before the Passion narrative begins — recapitulating the prologue's light-darkness imagery now grounded in the incarnate Christ's completed public ministry. The 'not abide in darkness' (mē meinē — subjunctive negative) Cyril takes as both promise and warning: the choice to abide in darkness is human refusal, not divine fate. Christ's coming as Light is for ALL; whether one walks in that Light is conditioned on faith. The verse provides the textual transition from public ministry (chapters 1-12) to the Farewell Discourses (chapters 13-17) in the Gospel's structure.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Jesus knew that His hour was come... having loved His own which were in the world, He loved them unto the end (eis telos)' Cyril takes as the thematic statement of the entire Last Supper / Farewell / Passion sequence. 'Unto the end' carries the double sense: temporally (to the very last moment of His earthly life and beyond) and qualitatively (to the perfect completion / telos of love). The 'His own' (tous idious) Cyril reads with theological precision: the chosen disciples who would become the apostolic foundation of the Church, but extending in the wider sense to all who would be united to them through the Spirit. This single verse for Cyril controls the interpretive horizon of the entire foot-washing-and-discourse complex that follows.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet' Cyril reads as the dominical institution of ecclesial humility. The verse is not (in Cyril's reading) the institution of a separate sacrament (against the medieval Latin pedilavium controversy that would come later) but the establishment of mutual humble service as the constitutive mark of Christian community. 'Ought' (opheilete) Cyril takes as moral obligation, not optional counsel. The Tewahedo Holy Week liturgy preserves the foot-washing ceremony on Holy Thursday — the Patriarch washes the feet of monks in deliberate enactment of this verse's pattern, modeling for the entire Church.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me' (citing Ps 41:9) Cyril reads as Christ's authoritative prophetic self-application of the Psalter. The verse establishes simultaneously: (1) Christ's foreknowledge of Judas's betrayal (refuting any reading that the cross was reactive surprise); (2) Christ's deliberate inclusion of Judas at the Supper (Judas receives the bread before going out — Cyril notes the eucharistic implications, though carefully); and (3) the messianic-prophetic reading of the Psalms as testimony to Christ (the Psalter's 'I' is appropriated by the messianic 'I'). The Tewahedo liturgical Psalter reads Psalm 41 with explicit Christological cross-reference per Cyril's pattern.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him' — spoken immediately after Judas's departure — Cyril reads as the inauguration of the glorification-sequence (cross-resurrection-ascension as a single glorifying movement). 'Glorified' (edoxasthē — aorist, completed action) Cyril takes proleptically: from the perspective of the divine will and economy, the work is already accomplished even as the historical events still unfold. The triple repetition of 'glorified' in vv. 31-32 Cyril takes as deliberate liturgical emphasis: the cross is glory, the resurrection is glory, the ascension is glory — one threefold glorification. This is the textual root of the Tewahedo Anaphora's pre-Sanctus doxology.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another' Cyril carefully expounds the 'newness' (kainēn) which the Mosaic commandment to love neighbor (Lev 19:18) had not abrogated. The newness consists in the CHRISTOLOGICAL measure ('as I have loved you') and in the new pneumatic capacity (the Spirit poured out makes possible what the law commanded). The 'as I have loved' Cyril reads as the love-of-Christ-for-His-Church (extending to the cross) being the operative pattern; Christian love is participatory imitation, not autonomous achievement. This verse anchors Cyril's ecclesiology: the Church is the community of those who love as Christ loved.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another' Cyril takes as Christ's missiological-apologetic instruction: the visible love-community of the Church is the primary evidential basis for the world's recognition of Christian truth. Not signs, not eloquence, not philosophical sophistication — LOVE for one another. 'All men' (pantes) Cyril reads as universal scope: this evidential love is not for in-house consumption but for the cosmos to witness. The Tewahedo monastic tradition preserves this verse as the controlling text for community life: the Synaxarium repeatedly notes saints whose distinguishing mark was conspicuous love for the brethren and the poor.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Let not your heart be troubled (mē tarassesthō): ye believe in God, believe also in me' Cyril notes the deliberate parallel of objects of faith: 'believe in God' and 'believe in me' (pisteuete eis ton Theon, kai eis eme pisteuete). The grammatical symmetry is Christological: faith in God and faith in Christ are not two different acts but one act with one object — the Triune God, in whose self-disclosure the Son is fully God. Against Arian readings that would distinguish 'belief in God' (proper) from 'belief in Christ' (subordinate), Cyril insists the parallel construction excludes any qualitative difference. The verse becomes a creedal pin for Tewahedo Trinitarian dogmatics.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'In my Father's house are many mansions (monai pollai)' Cyril reads with characteristic eschatological precision. The 'many' (pollai) Cyril takes as denying any uniform single eschatological reward: there are differentiated places-of-abiding corresponding to differentiated degrees of holiness attained. Yet he is careful against any Origenist universalism (which would make the differentiation purely educational on a unified upward path): the differentiation is permanent in the eschaton, not transitional. 'Father's house' Cyril reads as the totality of the kingdom, with the 'mansions' (literally 'abiding-places' — monai from menein, to remain) as the differentiated participation each saint has in the one beatific vision. This grounds the Tewahedo doctrine of the differentiated heavenly hierarchy of saints.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' is for Cyril the most exhaustive single-verse Christological self-disclosure in the Gospel. Each of the three predicates (the Way, the Truth, the Life) is paired with its corresponding human-need: the Way (for those who wander), the Truth (for those who err), the Life (for those who die). 'No man cometh unto the Father, but by me' Cyril takes as the textual root of Christological exclusivism: there is no Father-knowledge, no Father-relationship, no Father-presence available except through the Son. Against any reading that would permit alternative access (whether through other religions, through philosophical contemplation, or through natural ethics), Cyril insists on Johannine exclusivity. This verse anchors Tewahedo missiology.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He that hath seen me hath seen the Father' Cyril carefully unpacks against both Sabellian and Arian misreadings. Against Sabellians who would collapse the Persons: the verse does NOT identify the Son AS the Father (Cyril notes the immediate sequel: 'I am in the Father, and the Father in me' preserves the Personal distinction). Against Arians who would subordinate the Son: the verse asserts the Son's perfect representational adequacy — to see Him IS to see the Father, not partially or by analogy but fully and by nature. Cyril notes that the seeing in question is theological perception ('he that hath seen' = he that has truly recognized in faith), not merely physical optics. The verse grounds the Tewahedo iconographic tradition's confidence that depicting Christ's face is legitimate.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.1-3 (c. 350 AD)

'Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?' — Athanasius marks heōraken ton patera (hath-seen the Father) as the visibility-claim that follows from Jn 10:30's hen-esmen. To see the Son is to see the Father — not because Son and Father are the same-Person (modalism's mistake) and not because the Son is merely-an-image-of-the-Father (Arianism's mistake), but because the Son IS the eternal-eikōn-of-the-Father (Col 1:15) such that seeing the perfect-image is seeing the exact-substance the image perfectly reproduces. Athanasius pairs Jn 14:9 with Heb 1:3 (charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs autou — 'the express-image of his person') as the canonical-pair of perfect-eikōn-visibility verses. Tewahedo iconology cites Jn 14:9 as the Christological-warrant for the legitimacy of Christ-iconography (the Son's incarnate-circumscribability makes the Father's-eikōn depictable).

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am in the Father, and the Father in me' (egō en tō Patri, kai ho Patēr en emoi) is for Cyril the foundational Johannine text for what later Greek theology would call perichoresis: the mutual indwelling of the Persons of the Trinity. The reciprocal 'in' (en) preserves the Personal distinction (the Son is not the Father, the Father is not the Son) while affirming the consubstantial unity (each is fully in the other by virtue of the one shared divine essence). 'The words that I speak unto you, I speak not of myself' (continuing the verse) Cyril reads not as denial of personal agency but as expressing the unbroken Trinitarian operation: the Father's words come through the Son in the Spirit. This verse is the textual foundation of Cyril's Trinitarian theology.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I will pray the Father, and He shall give you another Comforter (allon Paraklēton), that He may abide with you for ever' is for Cyril the principal Johannine text on the personal divinity of the Holy Spirit. 'Another' (allon — implying same-kind-as) Cyril stresses: the Spirit is the same KIND of divine Person as Christ is — not a different ontological category, not a lesser being, not merely impersonal divine power. 'Paraklēton' Cyril expounds as advocate/comforter/encourager/intercessor — all four functions belong to the Spirit because they all belong to the divine Person. 'Abide with you for ever' establishes the permanence of the post-Pentecost Spirit-indwelling (as distinct from the intermittent prophetic-inspiration of the Old Covenant economy).

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Even the Spirit of truth (to Pneuma tēs alētheias); whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth Him not, neither knoweth Him' Cyril takes as the pneumatological criterion of saving knowledge. The world's incapacity to receive the Spirit Cyril attributes not to ontological lack but to the cognitive condition of unbelief that blocks perception. 'Ye know Him' (gnōskete) Cyril emphasizes as the disciples' present-tense possession of pneumatic knowledge — even before Pentecost, in nascent form. The eschatological 'shall be in you' (en hymin estai) Cyril reads as the post-Pentecost completion of what is here proleptically begun. Cyril's pneumatology of progressive economy (already present in the verse) becomes systematic in his On the Holy Trinity dialogues.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'At that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you' Cyril takes as the perichoretic extension to the Church: just as the Son is in the Father (Trinitarian mutual indwelling), so the believer is in the Son (ecclesial-mystical incorporation) and the Son in the believer (sacramental-Spiritual indwelling). The order is crucial for Cyril: the Trinitarian indwelling grounds the ecclesial, which grounds the Christological-in-the-individual. 'At that day' Cyril reads as the post-Pentecost age in which the Spirit's indwelling makes this triple participation effective. The Tewahedo Anaphora's epiclesis prayers explicitly invoke this triple participation as the gift the eucharistic communion realizes in the worshipper.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, He shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you' is for Cyril the locus classicus for the apostolic-authority basis of Scripture and Tradition. The Spirit's twin functions (teach + remind) presuppose the prior content given by Christ; the Spirit does not invent new revelation but illuminates and consolidates what Christ has spoken. This grounds Cyril's argument against any sectarian claim to revelation beyond the apostolic deposit: the Spirit's teaching is bounded by what Christ taught. The Tewahedo doctrine of the inseparability of Scripture-and-Tradition (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok + Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase together with the Tanakh + NT) rests on this Cyrilline reading.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My Father is greater than I' (ho Patēr meizōn mou estin) is THE most contested verse in Cyril's John commentary — the Arian polemical favorite throughout the 4th century, requiring careful orthodox exposition. Cyril resolves through the standard distinction: the verse predicates 'greater' of the Father with respect to the assumed humanity of the incarnate Son, NOT with respect to the eternal divine nature. Insofar as the Son is incarnate (took on human nature), the unincarnate Father is 'greater' in mode-of-existence; insofar as the Son is eternal Word, He is consubstantial-equal with the Father. The verse therefore confirms rather than denies the incarnation, and presupposes rather than undermines the consubstantiality. This careful exposition is one of Cyril's most-cited Johannine passages in later Greek theological tradition.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos I.58 (c. 350 AD)

'Ye have heard how I said unto you, I go away, and come again unto you. If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I' — Athanasius marks ho Patēr meizōn mou estin (the Father is greater than I) as the HARDEST ARIAN PROOFTEXT, addressed extensively at CA I.58-64. His resolution: 'greater' (meizōn) names the Father's-being-the-source / fount-of-deity (the unbegotten-pēgē, ho agennētos), while the Son is the begotten-from-Father (gegennēmenos ek tou Patros). The greater-than is RELATIONAL-ORIGIN, not substantial-inequality. The same-essence is communicated entirely-from-Father-to-Son; the Father is greater in the order-of-origination, not in the order-of-being. Pairs with Jn 10:30 (egō kai ho Patēr hen esmen — one in essence) as the canonical-Cappadocian-Athanasian source-without-subordination pair.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman' Cyril takes as the sixth of Christ's 'I AM' sayings and the foundational text for the doctrine of vital union between Christ and the Church. 'True' (alēthinē) Cyril emphasizes against any merely metaphorical or typological reading: Christ is not LIKE a vine, He IS the vine in the substantive sense — the source of life for the branches grafted into Him. The Father as 'husbandman' (geōrgos) Cyril reads as the Trinitarian operation in vine-tending: the Father's pruning and cultivating work is exercised through the Son in the Spirit. The Tewahedo Anaphora preserves this vine-husbandman language in its ecclesiological prayers.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing' is for Cyril the Christological-ecclesiological pin against any reading that would make Christian life autonomous. The reciprocal abiding (en emoi / en autō — in me / in him) Cyril takes as extending the Johannine perichoresis (14:10-11) from the Trinity to the Christ-Church relation by participation. 'Without me ye can do nothing' (chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden) Cyril takes with full force: not 'less effectively' but 'nothing at all' — every fruit-bearing in the Christian life is participatory in Christ's own activity. The verse is the textual foundation for the Tewahedo doctrine of synergism-in-grace: human cooperation is real but always sourced in prior divine indwelling.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends' Cyril reads as Christ's self-disclosure of the love that the cross will enact within hours. The 'greater' (meizona) establishes the comparative absolute: no love exceeds self-laying-down-for-friends. Christ's love for the world (Jn 3:16) is enacted as this love in the cross; the cross is therefore the visible measure of the previously-invisible Trinitarian love. 'For his friends' (hyper tōn philōn autou) Cyril reads with care: the love is universal in offer (15:16 'I have chosen you'), particular in friendship-bond. This anticipates the eucharistic ethic that becomes determinative for the Tewahedo monastic-martyrological tradition: laying-down-of-life is the Christian's proper response to having been thus loved.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit' Cyril takes as the dominical doctrine of election as priority of divine initiative. The reversal of expected ordering (the human disciple-choice is preceded and constituted by divine choice) Cyril reads as eliminating any boast: apostleship is gift, not achievement. 'Ordained' (ethēka — set / placed / appointed) Cyril notes carries the sense of sacramental commission: the appointment is not merely informational but operatively confers what it commissions. The Tewahedo doctrine of holy orders draws its theological warrant from this Cyrilline reading: ordination is participation in Christ's own ordaining act.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, He shall testify of me' is THE pneumatological text Cyril cites most heavily in his Trinitarian theology. The Greek ekporeuetai (proceedeth) Cyril reads as the eternal procession of the Spirit from the Father (the Eastern Orthodox foundation for the original Nicene formulation, against the later Western Filioque). Yet 'whom I will send' (pempsō egō) preserves the Son's role in the temporal mission of the Spirit. Cyril distinguishes carefully: the ETERNAL procession is from-the-Father-alone; the TEMPORAL mission is through-the-Son. This distinction becomes determinative for Eastern + Oriental Orthodox pneumatology, including Tewahedo.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'It is expedient (sympherei) for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send Him unto you' Cyril takes as the dominical pneumatology of progressive economy. Christ's bodily departure is necessary for the Spirit's coming because the modes of presence are different: Christ in the flesh was geographically limited (could be in one place at a time); the Spirit indwelling the Church is universally present everywhere His people gather. The 'expedient' (sympherei — beneficial / advantageous) Cyril emphasizes as not consolation-prize but actual upgrade: ascension + Spirit-coming is a richer mode of presence than incarnate proximity. The Tewahedo Anaphora's epiclesis prayers explicitly invoke this Cyrilline reading.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'When He, the Spirit of truth, is come, He will guide you into all truth: for He shall not speak of Himself; but whatsoever He shall hear, that shall He speak' Cyril unpacks against any reading that would make the Spirit a separate or supplementary teaching source. 'He shall not speak of Himself' Cyril reads as expressing perfect Trinitarian harmony: the Spirit's teaching IS the Father's + Son's teaching, mediated through the Spirit's distinctive operation, not a separate revelation. 'All truth' (eis tēn alētheian pasan) Cyril limits to the Christological-soteriological deposit: the Spirit guides into ALL the truth Christ has given, not into endless new revelations. This grounds patristic-Tewahedo apostolic-deposit doctrine.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Epistulae ad Serapionem 1.20 (c. 350 AD)

'Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come' — Athanasius marks the SPIRIT-OF-TRUTH ECONOMIC-MISSION as the Trinitarian-economy-of-revelation: the Spirit is sent-by-the-Son (who-is-the-truth, Jn 14:6), receives-from-the-Son (everything he speaks is from-the-Son), and guides-believers-into-the-Son. The Spirit's-procession-and-mission is Christo-centric in its economic-form. Jn 16:13 is the principal Johannine anchor for the doctrine that Letters to Serapion expounds: the Spirit, though distinct-Person from Father and Son, is homoousios with both and stands in unbroken-economic-coordination.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy' Cyril reads as the eschatological pattern of Christian experience: present suffering is not negated but transmuted by the resurrection. 'Turned' (genēsetai eis charan — shall be made into joy) Cyril takes literally: not 'replaced by' joy after sorrow ends, but TRANSFORMED INTO joy. The Easter pattern (Friday's sorrow becomes Sunday's joy through the cross-resurrection event) is the paradigm. Cyril applies this to every subsequent Christian experience of suffering: nothing in the Christian life is finally lost; every present sorrow is the seed of a future joy by participation in the paschal pattern. The Tewahedo Easter Anaphora preserves this transformative reading.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father' Cyril takes as the compressed Johannine summary of the entire incarnational economy. The four-fold movement (procession from Father / incarnation into world / departure from world / return to Father) Cyril reads as the dogmatic structure that the entire Gospel of John traces verse-by-verse. The 'came forth' (exēlthon) preserves the eternal procession; the 'come into the world' (elēlytha eis ton kosmon) marks the historical incarnation; the 'leave the world' (aphiēmi ton kosmon) anticipates the cross-and-ascension; the 'go to the Father' (poreuomai pros ton Patera) marks the consummation in glory. The Tewahedo Christmas Anaphora explicitly echoes all four movements.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee' opens the High-Priestly Prayer that Cyril treats with particular reverence — calling it 'the prayer the Church prays back to the Father along with Christ.' The 'hour' (hōra) Cyril reads as the kairos-hour of the entire incarnational economy: the appointed time toward which all prior events of Christ's life have been ordered. The mutual glorification (Son-glorified-by-Father and Father-glorified-by-Son) Cyril reads as preserving the Trinitarian symmetry: glory belongs to all three Persons, communicated reciprocally, never possessed monopolistically. This is the textual frame for the entire Tewahedo doxological tradition.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent' Cyril unpacks as the dominical definition of eternal life: not merely endless duration but cognitive-relational participation in the divine knowledge. The infinitive 'might know' (ginōskōsi — continuous action) Cyril takes as denoting ongoing personal knowing, not single intellectual grasp. The pairing (the Father AS only true God AND Jesus Christ AS sent) Cyril carefully reads to preserve both monotheism (against pagan polytheism) and Christological inclusion in deity (against Arian subordination): both clauses together constitute the saving knowledge. This verse anchors the Tewahedo catechetical tradition's definition of theosis as participation-by-knowing.
