◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was' (para seautō tē doxē hē eichon pro tou ton kosmon einai para soi) is Cyril's strongest single-verse text for the eternal pre-existence of the Son. 'Before the world was' Cyril takes against any Arian reading: the Son had glory WITH the Father before creation existed — therefore the Son's existence is not within creation's scope but eternal, alongside the Father from the very beginning. 'Thine own self' (para seautō) preserves the Personal distinction even within the consubstantial unity: the glory is shared between distinct Persons, not collapsed into Sabellian identity. This verse is among Cyril's most-cited prooftexts in the Twelve Anathemas against Nestorius.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.42 (c. 350 AD)

'And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was' — Athanasius marks tē doxē hē eichon pro tou ton kosmon einai para soi (the glory which I HAD with thee BEFORE the world was) as the DECISIVE pre-temporal-co-glory anchor: the Word's-glory is shared-with-the-Father before-the-cosmos-existed. Any creaturely glory-by-grace would be post-temporal (since creatures begin-to-be in time); only the Word, eternally-co-existent with the Father, can claim pre-temporal-shared-glory. The eichon (imperfect-tense, continuous-prior-state) excludes any 'gradually-acquired' Arian reading. Pairs with Jn 1:1 (en archē ēn ho Logos, kai ho Logos ēn pros ton theon) as the canonical pre-temporal-co-existence pair. The Tewahedo Doxology preserves this pre-temporal-glory in the Gloria-Patri-pattern: 'as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be.'

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth' Cyril takes as the dominical pin for the Word-mediated character of sanctification. 'Sanctify' (hagiason — set apart, make holy) Cyril reads as not merely declarative (treated as holy) but operatively transformative (actually made holy). The instrument of sanctification ('through thy truth') Cyril identifies as the apostolic Word given by Christ to the Church — the deposit that the Spirit teaches into all truth (16:13). The closing 'thy word is truth' Cyril takes with full force: the Word (the eternal Logos) IS the truth, and the spoken word (the apostolic Scripture) participates in that truth. This grounds the patristic-Tewahedo doctrine of Scripture's truth as Christ's own truth mediated.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us' is for Cyril THE ecclesiological text of the entire Gospel. The unity asked for is participatory: ecclesial unity is grounded in and patterned after Trinitarian unity. 'As' (kathōs) Cyril reads as analogical (a real likeness preserved across the ontological difference between Trinitarian-unity-by-nature and ecclesial-unity-by-grace). 'That the world may believe' (hina ho kosmos pisteusē — closing the verse) Cyril takes as missiological warrant: the visible unity of the Church is the primary evidential basis for the Gospel's credibility. The Tewahedo communion's preserved liturgical unity across 1700 years draws its theological warrant from this verse.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory' Cyril takes as the dominical eschatological prayer. 'Be with me where I am' (hina hopou eimi egō kakeinoi ōsi met' emou) Cyril reads as the consummation of the entire salvific economy: the goal is not merely forgiveness or moral renewal but ETERNAL CO-PRESENCE with the incarnate Word. 'Behold my glory' (theōrōsi tēn doxan tēn emēn) Cyril takes as the visio Dei — the eternal vision of God in the glorified flesh of Christ. This grounds the Tewahedo eschatological tradition that pictures heaven as eternal participatory contemplation of Christ's glory, not as static reward.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's self-identification at the arrest — 'I am he' (egō eimi) followed by the arresting party going backward and falling to the ground — Cyril reads as the deliberate Johannine theophanic intrusion into the Passion narrative. The 'I AM' Cyril links to the divine self-disclosure (Ex 3:14 ego eimi ho ōn); the falling-back is the standard biblical reaction of the unholy when confronted with theophany (cf. Ezek 1:28, Rev 1:17). Cyril's theological point: even at the moment of voluntary self-surrender, Christ's divinity is manifested visibly. The arrest happens only because Christ permits it, not because the arresting party has the power to take Him.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's rebuke of Peter — 'The cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?' — Cyril takes as the deliberate Johannine inversion of the Synoptic Gethsemane prayer ('let this cup pass from me'). John omits the Gethsemane agony entirely; instead, Christ at the moment of arrest already speaks the conformed-will resolution: the cup will be drunk. The 'shall I not drink' (ou mē piō auto) is rhetorical question expecting affirmative answer: of course He will drink, because the Father has given it. Cyril reads this as confirming the perfect alignment of the Son's incarnate will with the Father's eternal will, even at the moment of greatest stress. This grounds Cyril's later argument for the integrity of Christ's human will (against Apollinarian denial).

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My kingdom is not of this world (ek tou kosmou toutou): if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence' Cyril takes as the dominical pin against any theocratic or revolutionary reading of Christ's mission. The kingdom's NOT-FROM-HENCE (ek — out of, sourced in) does not mean NOT-FOR-HERE: it means not deriving its character from this-world's power structures (force, military conquest, political dominance). The kingdom IS for the world, but it operates by different means (suffering love, persuasive truth, sacramental presence). Cyril's reading establishes the theological frame for the Tewahedo monastic tradition's withdrawal-from-political-power as the proper kingdom-ethic, while still affirming the kingdom's universal scope.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Pilate's question — 'What is truth?' (ti estin alētheia) — Cyril treats with characteristic theological tragedy. Truth Himself stands before Pilate (Christ is the truth per 14:6); Pilate fails to recognize what is right in front of him. Cyril notes the absence of any answer from Christ: the only proper response to a question that misses what is already self-evidently present is silence. Pilate's tragic moment becomes the prototype of every subsequent encounter with Christ where the questioner cannot or will not see what is before them. The Tewahedo Good Friday liturgy preserves this moment with particular weight; the question and the silence stand as the textual icon of unbelief.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's reply to Pilate — 'Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above' — Cyril takes as the comprehensive doctrine of divine sovereignty over even the Passion's executioners. Pilate's authority is real (not denied) but derivative (not autonomous): every act of the powerful is bounded by divine permission. 'Therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin' (continuing the verse) Cyril takes as establishing graduated responsibility within the system: the Sanhedrin who delivered Christ to Pilate bear greater responsibility than Pilate, who merely executes their judgment within the bounds of his secondary authority. This nuanced reading shapes the Tewahedo Holy Week liturgy's careful theological framing.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's words from the cross to His mother and the beloved disciple — 'Woman, behold thy son! ... Behold thy mother!' — Cyril reads at multiple levels. Literally, Christ provides for Mary's continued care after His death (the eldest son's filial obligation discharged even from the cross). Typologically, Cyril takes Mary as figure of the Church and John as figure of every disciple: in establishing John as Mary's son, Christ establishes the Church as the Mother of every believer + every believer as the Church's son. The Tewahedo Marian veneration (which is particularly developed compared to other Christian traditions) draws its theological warrant from this Cyrilline reading.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's dying word — 'It is finished' (tetelestai) — Cyril takes as the dominical declaration of completed accomplishment. The perfect tense (tetelestai — completed action with continuing result) Cyril emphasizes: the work IS finished, definitively and abidingly. NOT 'I am dying' or 'I have failed' but 'the work is complete.' Cyril reads this as encompassing: the entire prophetic-typological economy of the Old Testament now fulfilled; the redemptive work for which the Word became flesh now consummated; the price for sin now paid in full. 'He bowed His head, and gave up the ghost' Cyril notes the order: Christ acts (bows head, gives spirit) — He is not passively overtaken by death but actively releases His life. The cross is sovereign self-offering, not victim's defeat.

On the blood and water from Christ's pierced side, Cyril reads sacramentally: the water signifies baptism, the blood signifies the eucharist, both flowing from the wound that is the source of the Church's life. The Tewahedo liturgical tradition preserves this dual symbolism with particular emphasis in the Anaphora of Our Lord Jesus Christ; the wound is the Church's font and table.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

John's interpretive comment — 'For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken' (citing Ex 12:46 / Num 9:12 / Ps 34:20) — Cyril takes as decisive paschal typology. The Passover lamb's prohibition on broken bones is fulfilled in the crucifixion's NOT-broken-bones (against the standard practice of breaking the legs to hasten death — done to the two thieves but providentially omitted for Christ). Cyril reads this as the divine providential ordering of even the smallest details of the Passion to display the Christ-as-Paschal-Lamb typology. The Tewahedo Passover-Easter liturgical complex preserves this typological reading prominently in its hymnody.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The Risen Christ's words to Mary Magdalene — 'Touch me not (mē mou haptou); for I am not yet ascended to my Father' — Cyril treats with care. The 'touch me not' Cyril reads not as ritual-purity concern (the resurrection-flesh is not unclean) but as redirecting Mary's grasping affection: the post-resurrection relationship will be different in mode, mediated through the ascension and the Spirit's coming. 'I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God' Cyril reads with careful Trinitarian precision: the distinction (MY Father / YOUR Father) preserves the Son's unique-by-nature sonship as distinct from the believers' adoptive-by-grace sonship. The verse establishes the theological basis for the Tewahedo doctrine of adoptive theosis.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'And when He had said this, He breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost' Cyril treats as a Trinitarian-pneumatological text of extraordinary density. The breathing (enephysēsen — the same verb as in Gen 2:7 LXX, where God breathes life into Adam) Cyril reads as the deliberate new-creation parallel: the Risen Christ inaugurates the eschatological new creation by breathing the Spirit into the new humanity. The 'Receive ye the Holy Ghost' (labete Pneuma Hagion) Cyril carefully distinguishes from Pentecost: this is the Spirit-gift FOR the apostolic commission (immediately followed by 'Whose soever sins ye remit'), Pentecost is the Spirit-gift for universal indwelling. Both are real; both are sourced in Christ. The Tewahedo holy-orders prayer at episcopal consecration echoes this verse explicitly.

◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.26 (c. 350 AD)

'And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God' — Athanasius marks ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou (the dual-vocative with definite articles) as the unambiguous post-resurrection divinity-confession. The grammar excludes every Arian-subordinationist reading: Thomas does NOT say 'a lord and a god' (indefinite, which a creature might receive) but 'THE Lord and THE God' (definite, the singular kyrios who is THE theos). Christ accepts the confession with a beatitude (Jn 20:29 makarioi hoi mē idontes — 'blessed are they that have not seen and yet have believed') — divine-acceptance of divine-worship that would be idolatry-by-Christ if he were a creature. The Tewahedo Easter (Fāsika) liturgical-acclamation cites Jn 20:28 at the second post-resurrection Sunday (Mansǝʿu — 'Risen-One') as the Thomine-confession-of-faith.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' Cyril takes as the dominical pin for faith-without-direct-evidence as the normative Christian condition. The Risen Christ does NOT rebuke Thomas's prior demand for evidence (the wounds are shown, the touch is offered); but He does proleptically commend the future generations whose faith will rest on apostolic testimony rather than direct sensory verification. The 'blessed' (makarioi) Cyril reads as ranking apostolic-testimony-based faith on the same scale as direct-sight faith — perhaps even higher, since it operates with less crutch. This grounds the entire Tewahedo catechetical-apologetic tradition that proclaims the Gospel as worthy of faith based on apostolic testimony.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The threefold question — 'Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?' — Cyril reads as the deliberate counterpart to Peter's threefold denial. Christ's repetition is restorative, not accusatory: each affirmation of love undoes one denial. 'More than these' (pleon toutōn) Cyril reads as referring to the other disciples (Peter had boasted in 13:37 that he would die for Christ even if all others fell away — Christ now tests the boast). The Greek verbal play (agapē / phileō) Cyril notes but treats with characteristic restraint: both verbs in John often function as synonyms; the deeper distinction is in the questioning-and-answering pattern itself, not in word-choice subtleties.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Feed my sheep' (boske ta probata mou) — the third and culminating commission to Peter — Cyril takes as the dominical institution of the pastoral office. The shift from 'lambs' (arnia, in v. 15) to 'sheep' (probata, in v. 17) Cyril reads as moving from the inexperienced new converts to the mature flock — the entire spectrum of pastoral responsibility is committed to Peter and through him to every subsequent pastor. The repetition Cyril sees as marking the deliberate sacramental-commissioning weight: this is not casual exhortation but solemn appointment. The Tewahedo ordination of bishops and priests preserves this verse's institutional weight in its consecration prayers.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome (nenikēka) the world' is for Cyril the closing dominical pin of the Farewell Discourses. The perfect tense 'have overcome' (nenikēka — completed action with continuing result) Cyril takes proleptically: the victory is spoken of as already accomplished from the perspective of the eternal Word, even though the cross-and-resurrection still lay ahead historically. 'Be of good cheer' (tharseite — take courage, be confident) is therefore not consolation despite-defeat but participatory rejoicing-in-victory: the disciples are invited to share Christ's confidence that the outcome is settled. This grounds the Tewahedo martyrological tradition's characteristic theological confidence.

epub:type="footnote">

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'And ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning' Cyril takes as the apostolic-foundation text grounding the historical-witness character of the Christian message. 'From the beginning' (ap' archēs) Cyril reads as the public-ministry beginning (from the Baptist's witness onward) — the apostles' qualification to bear witness rests on direct historical eyewitness, not on personal religious experience alone. This grounds the patristic-Tewahedo doctrine of apostolic succession: the Church's authoritative teaching traces back through a continuous chain to the eyewitness apostles, who saw with their own eyes what they then proclaimed.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him' — for Cyril this Baptist's final discourse is also a Christological confession: the Son is the criterion of judgment. 'Hath' (echei, present tense) Cyril stresses: eternal life is not merely future promise but present possession of the believer through union with Christ. 'Abideth' (menei) for the wrath similarly denotes present condition, not future sentence: unbelief is itself the judgment, since refusing the Son cuts off from the only source of life. Cyril here grounds the realized-eschatology dimension of Johannine theology against any purely futurist readings.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man' Cyril reads as the Christological fulfillment of Jacob's ladder vision (Gen 28:12): the incarnate Christ IS the ladder uniting heaven and earth in His own Person. The angels' bidirectional movement signifies the restored communication between divinity and creation through the Word made flesh. Cyril notes that this is the first explicit messianic self-identification in John's Gospel ('Son of man') and that it grounds the entire subsequent series of theophanic 'I am' sayings.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance' (Lk 15:7), Cyril reads the more-joy-over-one-sinner-repenting as the canonical Lukan anchor of the heaven-rejoices doctrine: the conversion of a single soul is not a private-individual event but a cosmic-angelic celebration. The 'more joy' is not comparative-quantitative but pastoral-emphatic — Cyril preserves the divine preference for the rescuing-pattern. Tewahedo missionary-spirituality cites Lk 15:7 + Lk 15:10 (joy in the presence of the angels) as the canonical doubled-witness of the doctrine that the angelic host participates joyfully in each conversion; the Tewahedo evangelistic-prayer tradition invokes the angels' rejoicing.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable of the lost coin — 'Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' (Lk 15:8) — Cyril reads the maternal-housekeeping-image as the canonical Lukan anchor of a doctrine that complements the shepherd-image (Lk 15:4) and the father-image (Lk 15:11): God seeks the lost in three iconic ways — shepherd seeking on the hills, woman seeking in the house, father waiting at the door. The triple-image is Trinitarian-iconic-pedagogy. Tewahedo Trinitarian-iconography cites Lk 15:4-32 as the canonical Lukan iconographic triple-pattern of the Father-Son-Spirit's-shared-search-for-the-lost.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable's opening 'A certain man had two sons' (Lk 15:11), Cyril reads the two-sons frame as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the parable's THIRD pivot (after shepherd + housekeeper) gives the Father his speaking-part: the father whose first speech is the silent embrace at 15:20, whose second speech is the celebration-command, whose third is the explanation to the elder brother. The full-pericope (Lk 15:11-32) is Christ's most-extended-character-development parable; the father's character is most-fully-disclosed. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 15:11-32 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Father's threefold-speech-of-mercy — the priest who absolves speaks as the father in the parable speaks.

On the master's commendation of the unjust steward — 'the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely' (Lk 16:8) — Cyril reads the lord-commended-the-unjust paradox as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that prudent-shrewdness in temporal matters should be matched by prudent-shrewdness in eternal matters: the steward is praised not for his dishonesty but for his foresight in securing his future. Tewahedo stewardship theology cites Lk 16:8 + Lk 16:9 ('make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of strategic-almsgiving — the prudent Christian uses temporal wealth to build eternal friendships (the recipients of the alms welcome the giver into eternal habitations).

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'No servant can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon' (Lk 16:13), Cyril reads the impossibility-formula (ou dynasthe — 'ye CANNOT') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the metaphysical incompatibility of God and mammon as objects-of-ultimate-loyalty: the disjunction is not pastoral counsel but ontological fact. Cyril notes the personification of mammon (treated as a rival lord) anticipates later patristic identifications of mammon-greed as a demonic principality. Tewahedo asceticism cites Lk 16:13 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that monastic poverty is the only consistent answer to the impossibility-formula — the bahǝtawi physically forecloses the option of serving mammon.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable's opening 'There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day' (Lk 16:19), Cyril reads the unnamed-rich-man + named-Lazarus contrast as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the reversal-of-recognition: the rich man (anonymous in the parable, anonymous in heaven) has his fine-linen reversed to torment; the poor man Lazarus (named, known to God) has his sores reversed to glory. The parable is Christ's most-vivid teaching on the post-mortem intermediate state — the doctrine elaborated at 16:23 seed. Tewahedo intermediate-state theology cites Lk 16:19 + Lk 16:23 + Lk 23:43 (good thief) as the canonical Lukan triple-witness for the conscious-intermediate-state of departed souls.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Cyril reads the Rich-Man-and-Lazarus narrative as canonically settling several intermediate-state questions: that there is consciousness after death; that the just are gathered to a place of refreshment ('Abraham's bosom'); that the unjust suffer torment in conscious recognition; that the chasm fixed between the two is uncrossable; that Moses and the Prophets are sufficient witnesses to deter the living. Tewahedo eschatology draws on Lk 16:19-31 as the principal canonical Lukan anchor of the intermediate-state doctrine.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the apostles' petition 'Lord, increase our faith' (Lk 17:5), Cyril reads the prosthes-hēmin-pistin (add-to-us-faith) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that faith is a gift to be asked for, not a quality to be produced: the apostles do not say 'we will work harder' but 'Lord, give us more'. Christ's mustard-seed answer (Lk 17:6) does not rebuke the request but redirects it — faith's POWER is not in its quantity but in its OBJECT (God's omnipotence). Tewahedo faith-formation cites Lk 17:5 + Lk 17:6 as the canonical doubled-Lukan-witness that faith is request-receivable from God (not striven-produced by self) and small-but-real-faith is sufficient if its object is the true God.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do' (Lk 17:10), Cyril reads the unprofitable-servants-formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of grace-against-merit: even maximal Christian-virtuous-action puts the disciple no further than baseline-duty; salvation is never owed to the disciple. The Greek achreioi (unprofitable, but also 'without-superfluous-claim') captures the disposition of the just-debtor with no surplus. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 17:10 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the monk's perpetual-humility-formula — 'I am an unprofitable servant' is recited in the daily-office.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Only the Samaritan among the ten cleansed lepers returns to give thanks at Christ's feet, and Cyril reads the verse as the canonical Lukan anchor of the eucharistic posture: the cleansed turn back to the cleanser in thanksgiving (eucharistia). The nine who do not return are not cured of the deeper leprosy of ingratitude. Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the Cyrillian reading: the proper response to divine cleansing is the return-to-the-altar with thanks.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'the kingdom of God is within you' (Lk 17:21 — entos hymōn estin), Cyril reads the entos-hymōn (within-you or among-you) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the present-immanent-kingdom: in Christ's person and ministry, the kingdom has already arrived among the questioners — the Pharisees see-but-do-not-recognize it. Cyril allows both readings (within = interior reign of God in the believer; among = Christ-the-kingdom-present-among). The Greek is deliberately ambiguous. Tewahedo theology of the kingdom cites Lk 17:21 + Mk 1:15 ('the kingdom of God is at hand') as the canonical doubled-witness for the already-present (Christological) and the still-coming (eschatological) dimensions of the kingdom.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's terse warning 'Remember Lot's wife' (Lk 17:32), Cyril reads the imperative-of-memory (mnēmoneuete) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that disobedient-looking-back is a paradigmatic-fatal-sin: Lot's wife (Gen 19:26) is preserved in canonical-memory not as a personal-name but as a warning-icon. The eschatological context (Lk 17:31 — that day, the rooftop) makes the warning explicit: when the kingdom comes, no looking-back. Tewahedo eschatological-asceticism cites Lk 17:32 + Lk 9:62 (plough-no-looking-back) as the canonical doubled-Lukan-witness for the irreversibility-of-disciple-orientation — both verses use the same forward-orientation grammar.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Luke's editorial introduction to the unjust-judge parable — 'he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint' (Lk 18:1) — Cyril reads the dei-pantote-proseuchesthai (it-is-necessary-always-to-pray) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of ceaseless-prayer (later codified by Paul at 1 Th 5:17 — 'pray without ceasing'). The grammatical necessity (dei) puts ceaseless-prayer on the same canonical level as 'must-be-baptized' and 'must-suffer'. Tewahedo monastic-prayer-discipline cites Lk 18:1 + 1 Th 5:17 as the canonical doubled-witness for the seven-fold daily office (Mäshafä Sǝʾatat) — seven daily prayer-points are the canonical operationalization of 'always pray, never faint'.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Pharisee's self-praising prayer 'God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are' (Lk 18:11), Cyril reads the Pharisee's-prayer as the canonical Lukan anti-model: addressed-to-God-in-form but self-praising-in-content. The prepositional pros-heauton (with-himself / to-himself — preferred reading) makes the Pharisee's prayer self-directed even in posture. Tewahedo confessor's-prayer-formation cites Lk 18:11 + Lk 18:13 (the Publican's prayer — seed γ.4.3) as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the two-prayer-patterns: the wrong one (Pharisee, self-praise) and the right one (Publican, 'God be merciful to me a sinner' — the Jesus-Prayer of Tewahedo monastic-spirituality).

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's mission-statement at the Zacchaeus episode 'For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost' (Lk 19:10), Cyril reads the doubled-mission (seek + save) as the canonical Lukan summary-statement of the Incarnation's purpose: the Son of Man's earthly trajectory (already-emphasized at Lk 5:32 — come to call sinners) reaches its compact-definitive expression here. The verse becomes load-bearing for the patristic doctrine of the missio Dei — God's outgoing mission preceding any human response. Tewahedo missionary theology cites Lk 19:10 + Lk 5:32 as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the doctrine that Christian mission participates in the dominical-search-and-rescue mission; the Tewahedo apostolic-outreach to the Beta-Israel and surrounding peoples is the appropriation of this canonical pattern.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the triumphal-entry cry 'Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest' (Lk 19:38), Cyril reads the Lukan-distinctive 'peace in heaven' (where the Synoptic parallels say 'Hosanna in the highest') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the cosmic-reconciliation announcement: heaven-and-earth peace is the explicit content of Christ's triumphal-entry. The phrase echoes the angelic Christmas-hymn (Lk 2:14 — peace-on-earth) and now reverses: peace-on-earth then, peace-in-heaven now. Tewahedo Hosanna-procession (Hosanna feast — the Sunday before Pascha) cites Lk 19:38 alongside Lk 2:14 as the canonical Lukan-doubled-witness of the peace-of-the-incarnation completed at the Cross.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Christ's weeping over Jerusalem is for Cyril the canonical disclosure of the Lord's mercy precisely toward the city about to reject him. The tears do not soften the prophetic announcement of the city's destruction; they intensify it as the announcement of a real and grievous loss. Cyril rejects every reading that would treat the tears as mere stagecraft. Tewahedo Holy-Week lectionary preserves Lk 19:41-44 as the Palm-Sunday-eve reading of the Lord's lament.

On Christ's cleansing of the Temple — 'It is written, My house is the house of prayer: but ye have made it a den of thieves' (Lk 19:46) — Cyril reads the citation of Isa 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the consecrated-place is by-definition the house-of-prayer; commerce within the precinct DEFILES the consecration. Christ's action is canonical-prophetic, not anti-Temple in principle (Christ continues to teach there daily, Lk 19:47). Tewahedo church-discipline cites Lk 19:46 + Is 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical triple-witness that the church-building is by definition the house-of-prayer; commercial use of the precinct (vending, money-changing) is excluded by canonical prophet-and-dominical authority.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Temple-elders' challenge 'by what authority doest thou these things?' (Lk 20:1-2), Cyril reads the authority-question as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's authority is self-authenticating, not derived from human institutions: the Lord refuses to license his actions to the question-form because to do so would already concede that authority is delegable by the Sanhedrin. Christ's counter-question about John's baptism (Lk 20:4) traps the elders in their own institutional logic. Tewahedo ecclesial theology cites Lk 20:1-8 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Church's authority traces to Christ directly, not through Imperial-Sanhedrin-style human delegation.

On the parable of the wicked husbandmen (Lk 20:9-16), Cyril reads the vineyard-tenants who reject the servants and finally kill the heir as the canonical Lukan anchor of the salvation-history-as-progressive-rejection: prophets sent, prophets killed; finally the Son sent, the Son killed; the vineyard given to others (Gentiles + Tewahedo). Tewahedo missionary-theology cites Lk 20:9-16 + Mt 21:43 ('the kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the Gentile-Ethiopian inclusion in the vineyard is the consequence of the canonical-prophetic rejection of Christ at Calvary.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's' — Cyril treats the saying as the canonical two-spheres principle: civic duty is real but subordinate, and never displaces the duty to God. The denarius carries Caesar's image; the soul carries God's. The implicit argument is that the soul is rendered to God by being conformed to his image. Tewahedo political theology cites Lk 20:25 as the canonical two-kingdoms anchor.

On Christ's 'For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him' (Lk 20:38), Cyril reads the all-live-unto-him (pantes gar autō zōsin — Luke's distinctive addition over Mark/Matthew) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the patriarchs whom God identifies himself with (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) are alive-to-God right now — not merely scheduled-for-future-resurrection. The intermediate-state of the righteous is conscious-life-with-God. Tewahedo intermediate-state-theology cites Lk 20:38 as the canonical Lukan anchor doubled with Lk 16:23 (Lazarus in Abraham's bosom) and Lk 23:43 (today thou shalt be with me in paradise) — the conscious-life-with-Christ of the departed righteous is canonically witnessed three-times in Luke alone.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's puzzle from Psalm 110 — 'David himself saith in the book of Psalms, The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand' (Lk 20:42, citing Ps 110:1) — Cyril reads the Psalm-110 citation as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Christological double-Lordship: David (the messiah's ancestor) addresses the messiah AS HIS LORD, which makes the messiah more than merely David's son. Ps 110:1 becomes the most-cited Old-Testament verse in the New Testament (~25 times) and the foundational text for Christ's session at the Father's right hand (Ascension theology). Tewahedo Christology cites Lk 20:42 + Ps 110:1 as the canonical Old-Testament-Christological double-Lordship anchor; the Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the right-hand-of-the-Father language verbatim.

On Christ's word to the arresting-officers 'this is your hour, and the power of darkness' (Lk 22:53), Cyril reads the doubled-phrase (your-hour + power-of-darkness) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Satan-permitted-darkness-hour: the Passion proceeds not because Christ is defeated but because the Father permits the hour of the powers-of-darkness. The exousia tou skotous (authority of darkness) is the same authority Christ acknowledges at his arrest as permitted but not victorious. Tewahedo Holy-Week theology cites Lk 22:53 + Col 1:13 (delivered from the power of darkness) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the Cross goes through the darkness-hour to the resurrection-light.

On Peter's Lukan-distinctive response after the cock-crow — 'And Peter went out, and wept bitterly' (Lk 22:62) — Cyril reads the eklausen pikrōs (wept bitterly) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of repentant-tears as the active-receptive expression of post-fall sorrow: tears are not despair but the moisture of returning-love. Peter's tears are the inverse of Judas's hanging (Mt 27:5); the same betrayal, different response. ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Jerusalem-mob's cry 'Crucify him, crucify him' (Lk 23:21), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative as the canonical Lukan anchor of the canonical-prophetic-rejection's voice: the cry that reverses the Hosanna of Lk 19:38 by the same population. Cyril is careful to distinguish the city-political mob from 'the Jewish people' as a whole (against any later anti-Judaic reading); the cry is the act of a Jerusalem-Caiaphas-orchestrated faction. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 23:21 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the same human voice can ascribe Hosanna-and-Crucify within a single week — the warning against fickle-religiosity.

'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do' — Cyril treats the first word from the Cross as the canonical fulfilment of Is 53:12 ('he made intercession for the transgressors'). The intercessory office of the High Priest is exercised from the altar of the Cross itself. The 'they know not' is a real plea for ignorance-extenuation: those who execute Christ are bidden to the same forgiveness offered to all. Tewahedo Good-Friday liturgy preserves Lk 23:34 at the head of the seven words.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the good-thief's plea 'Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom' (Lk 23:42), Cyril reads the dying-thief's confession as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of last-moment-saving-faith: a sinner with no time for catechesis, no baptism, no works — yet his confession ('Lord' + recognition of the kingdom) suffices. Christ's answer (Lk 23:43 — seed entry) is the canonical promise; this verse is the canonical confession. Tewahedo pastoral-theology of last-rites cites Lk 23:42 + Lk 23:43 as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness for the doctrine that the deathbed confession is salvifically-effective; the priest at the bedside follows the dominical pattern of the Christ-and-thief exchange.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise' — Cyril reads the promise to the good thief as the canonical anchor of three doctrines: (1) Christ retains the prerogative of paradise even at the moment of his apparent defeat; (2) confession-from-the-cross suffices for salvation; (3) the saints enter paradise immediately at death and do not wait. The 'today' rules out every reading that defers the saints' beatific reception to the Last Day alone. Tewahedo intermediate-state doctrine cites Lk 23:43 as a principal canonical anchor.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the cosmic-darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour (Lk 23:44), Cyril reads the three-hour-darkness as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the cosmic-participation in the Passion: creation darkens because its Maker dies. The three hours echo Jonah's three days in the fish (Mt 12:40), the three days Moses was in the ark (Jub 47:5), and the three days Christ will be in the tomb. Tewahedo cosmic-Christology cites Lk 23:44 + Mt 27:51-52 (earth-quake, rocks rent, graves opened) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the natural-cosmic-order participates in the death of its Word-Maker; the Tewahedo Holy-Friday liturgy preserves the three-hour darkening observance.

The veil rent from top to bottom (Mt 27:51) signals God's-direction rather than human-direction of the action. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 23:45 + Heb 10:19-20 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the iconographic-curtain in the Tewahedo sanctuary (which veils the maqdas) functions as both barrier-and-passage — the curtain that screens is also the curtain that opens at the Eucharistic moment.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the rich man's plea + Abraham's answer 'If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead' (Lk 16:31), Cyril reads Abraham's verdict as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the sufficiency-of-Scripture for salvation: even resurrection-witness will not persuade those who have hardened against the canonical word. The verse becomes load-bearing in the Lukan-Acts trajectory: the post-resurrection apostolic preaching cites the OT Scriptures as the basis of belief (Acts 17:11 — Bereans searched the Scriptures). Tewahedo bibliology cites Lk 16:31 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the canonical Scriptures are sufficient for salvation; private revelations and apparitions are accountable to that canonical word.

◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the father's final words to the elder brother 'It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found' (Lk 15:32), Cyril reads the doubled-formula (dead-and-alive + lost-and-found) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of conversion-as-resurrection: the prodigal's return is not merely moral-improvement but a passage from death to life. The same doubled-formula echoes Christian baptism (Rom 6:4 — dead with Christ, alive in Christ). Tewahedo baptismal-and-penance theology cites Lk 15:32 + Rom 6:4 as the canonical doubled-witness that every conversion is a participation in the death-and-resurrection of Christ; the Tewahedo penance-rite preserves the alive-again grammar in its absolution formula.
